blocks.content: Climate is one of the most important concepts in Geography. It represents the long-term average condition of the atmosphere of a place and controls almost every aspect of natural and human life. Climate is not decided by one factor alone but by the combined interaction of temperature, air pressure, winds, humidity and rainfall over a long period of time. This chapter is frequently asked in  examinations in the form of direct questions, classification-based MCQs, matching questions and conceptual questions.
PART A: BASIC CONCEPT OF CLIMATE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Weather refers to day-to-day atmospheric conditions, while climate represents long-term statistical averages over decades.
Key factors controlling climate include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief features, and prevailing winds.
Köppen's classification system categorizes world climates into five major broad groups: Tropical (A), Dry (B), Warm Temperate (C), Cold Temperate (D), and Polar (E).
Climatic conditions directly determine the distribution, type, and adaptation of natural vegetation across geographical regions.

blocks.content: Meaning of Climate

Climate refers to the average atmospheric conditions of a place observed over a long period of time, usually 30 years or more. It includes the study of temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure and wind patterns. Climate gives a general idea about the weather conditions that are expected in a region year after year.
Difference between Weather and Climate

Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. It changes frequently and can vary from hour to hour or day to day. Climate, on the other hand, is the long-term average of weather conditions. Weather is short-term, while climate is long-term in nature.
PART B: FACTORS AFFECTING CLIMATE
Latitude

Latitude is the most important factor affecting climate. Areas near the equator receive direct vertical rays of the Sun and therefore experience high temperatures throughout the year. As we move away from the equator towards the poles, the Sun’s rays become slanting, spread over a larger area and pass through a thicker layer of atmosphere, resulting in lower temperatures.
Altitude

Temperature decreases with increase in altitude because air becomes thinner and less capable of retaining heat. The normal lapse rate is 6.5°C per 1000 metres. This is why hill stations are cooler than nearby plains.
Distance from the Sea (Continentality)

Land heats and cools faster than water. Coastal areas experience moderate climate because the sea influences temperature. Interior areas far from the sea experience extreme temperatures, with very hot summers and very cold winters.
Ocean Currents

Ocean currents modify the climate of coastal regions. Warm ocean currents increase temperature and humidity, leading to higher rainfall, whereas cold ocean currents reduce temperature and often cause dry conditions.
Relief and Mountains
Mountains act as climatic barriers. They block the movement of winds and cause orographic rainfall on the windward side, while the leeward side experiences rain shadow conditions.
Prevailing Winds
Prevailing winds transport heat and moisture from one region to another. Winds coming from oceans bring moisture and rainfall, while winds coming from land are generally dry.
PART C: CLASSIFICATION OF CLIMATE
Need for Climatic Classification

Climatic classification helps in grouping regions with similar climatic conditions. It makes the study of world climate systematic and useful for agriculture, planning, settlement and environmental studies.
Köppen’s Classification of Climate

Köppen’s climatic classification is the most widely used system in the world. It is based on temperature and rainfall and their seasonal distribution. Köppen divided the world into five major climatic groups.
Major Climatic Groups According to Köppen
Tropical Climates (Group A)
Tropical climates are found near the equator and experience high temperatures throughout the year. Rainfall is generally heavy.

blocks.content: Af – Tropical Rainforest Climate: Rainfall throughout the year. Am – Tropical Monsoon Climate: Seasonal heavy rainfall.
Aw – Tropical Savanna Climate: Wet and dry seasons.
Dry Climates (Group B)
Dry climates are characterised by very low rainfall where evaporation exceeds precipitation.
Types of Dry Climate BW – Desert Climate. BS – Steppe Climate.
Warm Temperate Climates (Group C)
These climates have mild winters and warm summers.
Types of Warm Temperate Climate
Cs – Mediterranean Climate (dry summer, wet winter). Cf – Marine West Coast Climate.
Cw – China Type Climate.
Cold Temperate Climates (Group D)
Cold temperate climates experience severe winters and short summers. Taiga climate is a major example.
Polar Climates (Group E)

PART D: CLIMATE AND NATURAL VEGETATION

Climate directly controls the type of natural vegetation. Hot and wet climates support dense forests, dry climates support deserts, temperate climates support grasslands and forests, and polar climates support tundra vegetation.
PART E: IMPORTANCE OF CLIMATE
Climate influences agriculture, water resources, settlement patterns, industries, biodiversity and human health. Understanding climate is essential for disaster management and climate change studies.
